### lambda-account-rps-10000-default

**Claim.** Across all functions in an account, Lambda enforces a requests-per-second limit of 10 times the account concurrency, so with the default concurrency limit of 1,000 the functions can handle at most 10,000 requests per second.

**Write it as.** `10,000 requests per second` · `10 times your account concurrency`

**Scope.** per account, all functions together; default; adjustable; at the default account concurrency limit.

> "Across all functions in your account, Lambda enforces a requests per second limit that's equal to 10 times your account concurrency. For example, since the default account concurrency limit is 1,000, functions in your account can handle a maximum of 10,000 requests per second."
> — [Understanding Lambda function scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-concurrency.html)

### lambda-addpermission-limited-condition-keys

**Claim.** Individual permissions added with the console or the AddPermission API are single Allow statements that support only aws:SourceArn, aws:SourceAccount and aws:PrincipalOrgID as condition keys; a full JSON policy (PutResourcePolicy) supports all IAM global condition keys, multiple principals and explicit Deny statements.

**Write it as.** `add single Allow statements` · `only a limited set of condition keys` · `create explicit Deny statements`

**Scope.** function resource-based policy.

> "Individual permissions – Use the console or AddPermission API action to add single Allow statements. Individual permissions support only a limited set of condition keys (aws:SourceArn, aws:SourceAccount, and aws:PrincipalOrgID)."

> "With a full JSON policy, you can use the complete range of IAM global condition keys, add multiple statements with multiple principals, and create explicit Deny statements."
> — [Working with resource-based policies in Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/access-control-resource-based.html)

### lambda-async-sns-destination-256-kb

### lambda-bp-runaway-reserved-zero

> "Avoid using recursive invocations in your Lambda function, where the function invokes itself or initiates a process that may invoke the function again. This could lead to unintended volume of function invocations and escalated costs. ### lambda-chaining-anti-pattern-sqs-or-step-functions

**Claim.** Lambda functions directly calling other Lambda functions is generally an anti-pattern because of cost and complexity (except for durable functions); the two common alternatives are an Amazon SQS queue between the functions or AWS Step Functions.

**Write it as.** `generally an anti-pattern` · `use an Amazon SQS queue between Lambda functions` · `use AWS Step Functions`

**Scope.** Lambda application design; does not apply to durable functions.

> "While Lambda functions directly calling other Lambda functions is generally an anti-pattern due to cost and complexity concerns, this doesn't apply to durable functions, which are specifically designed to orchestrate multi-step workflows by invoking other functions."
> — [Creating event-driven architectures with Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/concepts-event-driven-architectures.html)

> "In serverless applications, there are two common approaches to avoid this pattern. First, use an Amazon SQS queue between Lambda functions. If a downstream process is slower than an upstream process, the queue durably persists messages and decouples the two functions."
> — [Creating event-driven architectures with Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/concepts-event-driven-architectures.html)

> "The second approach is to use AWS Step Functions."
> — [Creating event-driven architectures with Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/concepts-event-driven-architectures.html)

### lambda-chaining-cost-wait-state

**Claim.** With Lambda you pay for the duration of an invocation, so in a chain of synchronous calls the calling functions keep running in a wait state while the last function runs, and their concurrency must all be equal.

**Write it as.** `you pay for the duration of an invocation` · `running in a wait state`

**Scope.** Lambda application design.

> "Cost – With Lambda, you pay for the duration of an invocation. In this example, while the Create invoice functions runs, two other functions are also running in a wait state, shown in red on the diagram."
> — [Creating event-driven architectures with Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/concepts-event-driven-architectures.html)

> "Scaling – The concurrency of all three functions must be equal. In a busy system, this uses more concurrency than would otherwise be needed."
> — [Creating event-driven architectures with Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/concepts-event-driven-architectures.html)

### lambda-warm-start-environment-reuse

**Claim.** After an invocation the execution environment is frozen and kept for a period of time; if another request for the same function arrives, Lambda can reuse the environment, which is called a warm start and typically finishes more quickly.

**Write it as.** `Lambda can reuse the environment` · `warm start` · `the execution environment is frozen`

**Scope.** per execution environment.

> "After the invocation completes, the execution environment is frozen. To improve resource management and performance, Lambda retains the execution environment for a period of time. During this time, if another request arrives for the same function, Lambda can reuse the environment. This second request typically finishes more quickly, since the execution environment is already fully set up. This is called a "warm start"."
> — [Understanding the Lambda execution environment lifecycle](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-runtime-environment.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-10.

### lambda-xray-active-tracing

**Claim.** Lambda supports the X-Ray tracing modes Active and PassThrough; with Active tracing Lambda automatically creates trace segments for invocations and sends them to X-Ray, and the execution role needs permission to upload trace data (the console adds it, or attach AWSXRayDaemonWriteAccess).

**Write it as.** `Active and PassThrough` · `automatically creates trace segments` · `AWSXRayDaemonWriteAccess`

**Scope.** Lambda with AWS X-Ray.

> "Lambda supports two tracing modes for X-Ray: `Active` and `PassThrough`. With `Active` tracing, Lambda automatically creates trace segments for function invocations and sends them to X-Ray."
> — [Visualize Lambda function invocations using AWS X-Ray](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-xray.html)

> "Your function needs permission to upload trace data to X-Ray. When you activate tracing in the Lambda console, Lambda adds the required permissions to your function's execution role. Otherwise, add the AWSXRayDaemonWriteAccess policy to the execution role."
> — [Visualize Lambda function invocations using AWS X-Ray](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-xray.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-13.
